query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for demanding engineering applications, the retention or loss of toughness is governed by the degree and nature of grain‐boundary chemistry: modest segregation of selected minor elements enhances grain-boundary cohesion and retards crack initiation and propagation, whereas excessive segregation or the formation of brittle, grain-boundary precipitates undermines toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a nearly homogeneous elemental distribution and a baseline toughness measured under standard mechanical testing conditions.
generation.intervention: A series of controlled post-casting annealing treatments at increasing temperatures (or durations) designed to promote graded levels of grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Samples are subjected to identical mechanical testing (e.g., standardized fracture toughness tests and impact tests) at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures. Grain-boundary chemistry is characterized using TEM/EDS and atom-probe tomography before mechanical evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries whose local chemistry is modified by the controlled segregation of minor alloying elements (or formation of secondary precipitates) that affect intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At moderate annealing conditions, controlled segregation of certain elements enhances the local cohesion at grain boundaries, impeding crack nucleation and propagation, which results in retained or improved toughness. However, when annealing conditions drive excessive segregation or promote the formation of brittle precipitates at the boundaries, these sites become preferential crack paths that markedly reduce toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast, homogeneous baseline, samples subjected to moderate annealing (with beneficial grain-boundary segregation) will exhibit higher fracture toughness and greater resistance to crack propagation. Conversely, samples that are over-annealed (leading to extensive segregation or precipitate formation) will show a significant reduction in toughness and an increased tendency for intergranular fracture.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase HEA with homogeneous composition and measured toughness value under standardized fracture tests.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for HEAs within a practical processing window (annealing temperatures and durations that do not induce complete phase separation or melting), and for mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures relevant for demanding applications. Its applicability beyond these temperature regimes or for radically different compositions is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise annealing conditions (temperature/time thresholds) for the optimum segregation versus detrimental precipitate formation are not well defined and may vary with specific HEA compositions. The balance between beneficial minor-element segregation and harmful coarse precipitation requires further quantitative calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical HEA samples and subject them to a systematic annealing study. Use TEM/EDS and atom-probe tomography to quantify the extent and nature of grain-boundary segregation and any precipitate formation. Then, perform standardized fracture toughness and impact tests on each set of samples. Correlate the measured toughness with the observed grain-boundary chemistry and microstructural features.
measurements: Quantitative grain-boundary composition from TEM/EDS or atom-probe tomography
Presence, size, and volume fraction of any grain-boundary precipitates
Fracture toughness (K_IC) and impact test results under controlled temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the variation in grain-boundary chemistry and/or precipitate formation induced by the annealing treatment does not correlate with corresponding changes in fracture toughness relative to the as-cast baseline (i.e., if samples with pronounced segregation or precipitates do not exhibit predictable improvements or deteriorations in toughness), then the hypothesis that grain-boundary processes govern toughness retention or loss is falsified.
